payload.body:
You often discover what you think by talking, writing, asking questions, or hearing yourself explain a decision out loud. The way you describe yourself matters too, because what you say you are doing, where you say you are headed, and the story you keep repeating can become part of how other people learn to see you.

Your mind is close to the surface, so people usually get a sense of what interests you quickly. You ask questions, notice the detail that changes the meaning, or change your position when new information gives you a better answer. You do not need to pretend certainty just because you spoke first.

Words can start defining you before you have finished defining yourself. Something you said while figuring it out becomes the story other people repeat back to you, or an old description keeps following you after your thinking has changed.

Pay attention to how you narrate your own life. You are allowed to know more now than you knew when you first described the plan. Say what you can stand behind, and let your language change when your thinking does.
